module_title: State Executive - Discretionary Powers, Vetoes, and Centre-State Frictions
introduction: This advanced level analyzes the critical powers that distinguish the Governor from the President—specifically 'Constitutional Discretion'. It also explores how the Governor's role as a representative of the Centre frequently leads to Centre-State disputes.

core_concepts.title: Constitutional Discretion (Article 163)
core_concepts.description: Unlike the President, the Constitution explicitly gives the Governor 'Constitutional Discretion' (where they are not bound by the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers). Examples: Reserving a bill for the President's consideration (Art 200) and recommending President's Rule (Art 356).

core_concepts.title: Veto on Bills (Articles 200 & 201)
core_concepts.description: When a bill is sent to the Governor, they can: 1. Give assent, 2. Withhold assent, 3. Return it (if not a money bill), or 4. **Reserve it for the President (Art 200)**. Once a bill is reserved for the President, the Governor has no further role to play in its enactment (Art 201).

core_concepts.title: Situational Discretion
core_concepts.description: This is exercised by both the President and Governor in situations like: Appointing a CM when no party has a clear majority (Hung Assembly), or dismissing the council of ministers if they lose the majority in the house.

core_concepts.title: Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions
core_concepts.description: Commissions on Centre-State relations recommended that: The Governor should be an eminent person from OUTSIDE the state, should not be intimately connected with local politics, and should be appointed after consulting the Chief Minister.

important_entities.name: S.R. Bommai Case (1994)
important_entities.significance: It established that a Chief Minister's majority must be tested on the 'Floor of the House' (Legislative Assembly) and not subjectively assessed in the Raj Bhavan by the Governor. This curbed the misuse of Article 356.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a Governor reserves a state bill for the President, and the President returns it for reconsideration, even if the state legislature passes it again and sends it back, the President is NOT bound to give assent (unlike Central bills where the President is bound after reconsideration).
The Governor is 'obligated' (mandatory) to reserve a bill for the President if it endangers the position or powers of the State High Court. For other matters, it is discretionary.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: 200 to Hold, 201 for the President's Fold
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Under Article 200, the Governor 'holds' (reserves) the bill. Under Article 201, the President takes action on that reserved bill.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Assertion-Reasoning questions, critically analyze the difference between the 'Constitutional Discretion' of the Governor and the lack of it for the President.
The S.R. Bommai case is repeatedly asked regarding the limits of the Governor's power to recommend the dismissal of a state government.
